article_text:
40 years ago, the crime drama “ Heat ” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “ Heat ” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds , was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.”

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.)

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

The first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt said he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

The experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.
excerpt_original: Derived from a screenplay by the legendary William Goldman, this hard-boiled gem was unfairly forgotten almost as soon as it was released. Its 40th anniversary provides an opportunity to fix that.

article_text:
News

Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

Christie's withdraws a Frida Kahlo painting following protests, Sotheby's says heirs of contested Van Gogh agreed to a deal, and more in today's art news.

Bukowskis )

Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic's writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us .

Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “ Ser III No. 5 ” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis , which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist , with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized .

Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale

After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tonight when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.

article_text:
Cannes 2026 is in full swing and the Film Comment crew is on the ground, cutting through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more. This year’s edition is packed with highly anticipated premieres from Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, Valeska Grisebach, James Gray, Paweł Pawlikowski, and many more acclaimed filmmakers.

For our sixth Podcast from the sun-dappled shores of the French Riviera, Sight and Sound’ s Isabel Stevens and scholar Neta Alexander join FC Editor Devika Girish to share their responses to two Competition titles that are sure to generate lots of chatter: Cristian Mungiu’s legal thriller Fjord (3:15) and Pedro Almodóvar’s self-reflexive drama Bitter Christmas (19:25). Next, they turn to two highlights from the festival’s other sections: Austrian director Sandra Wollner’s Everytime (26:00), which premiered as part of Un Certain Regard, and Chilean filmmaker Dominga Sotomayor’s La perra (32:50), a selection in the Directors’ Fortnight program.

Subscribe today to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.

"paragraph", "text": "24日（土）は抗議デモが予定され、フェア会場である グラン・パレ 前での集会も呼びかけられていたため、この日の中止はやむを得ないとして広く受け入れられた。ところが、出展者の多くは、25日（日）にフェアが再開されなかったことに驚いたという。デモの予定はなく、グラン・パレの別会場でのセザンヌ展は再開されていたからだ。CPGAのフィリップ・シャルパンティエ会長は、フランス版アート・ニュースペーパー紙に対し、次のように語っている。", "links": "「土曜日の中止は全面的に支持します。前週末のデモで警備上の不手際があり、その後に深刻な騒乱が起きたことを思えば、絶対に必要な予防措置でした。ただ、日曜日には再開してほしいと伝える機会がなかったことが残念です」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一方のホロウィッツはCPGAの抗議に関し、「極めて流動的な状況の中で対応を迫られていました。フェア期間中も、その後の数週間も、多くのギャラリーと話し合いを重ね、私たちはそこから多くを学びました。どの事業者もそうであるように、さまざまなプロセスを改善し、今後はより良い対応ができるよう努めます」とUS版ARTnewsに述べ、日曜日に再開しなかった理由をこう付け加えた。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ホロウィッツはまた、「全体状況および当事者間の関係」について幅広く話し合うため、12月14日にアート・バーゼル・パリとCPGAの代表者が会合を持つ予定だと述べた。両者は定期的に会合を開いているが、今回は会期短縮による損害の補償についてアート・バーゼル経営陣との協議を求めたCPGAの要請を受けてのものだという。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会合には、フランス文化省とフェア会場であるグラン・パレの運営母体RMN-GP（フランス国立美術館連合−グラン・パレ）の代表者も出席する。両者はUS版ARTnewsの問い合わせに対し、会期短縮の補償としてのブース料減額には関与していないと回答。ホロウィッツも、アート・バーゼルがRMN-GPおよびフランス当局と結んだ契約や保険の内容についてはコメントできないとしている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "フランス文化省の広報担当者は声明で、「私たちの役割は建設的な対話の場をつくることです。それを通じて、ギャラリー、主催者、会場がそれぞれ受けた影響を把握し、今回の出来事から教訓を得ることが目的です」と強調している。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "フランス国外の中小ギャラリーは概ね早期閉幕への理解を示す"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "補償を正式に求めたのはCPGAだけではない。US版ARTnewsは、フランス国外に拠点を置く数十軒の中堅・小規模ギャラリーに、主催者側の対応について尋ねた。その結果、主催者は何らかの補償をすべきかとの質問には、全員が「はい」と答えている。一方、望ましい補償については、小規模ギャラリーへの補償を優先してほしいという意見から、当初の日程の3分の1が短縮されたのだからブース料金の3分の1を返金してほしいという要望まで、内容は多岐にわたった。中には、来年の出展料やブース料金に充当できるバウチャーを求める声もあった。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "これに対してホロウィッツは、将来のフェアで使える特典よりも「10月のフェアに出展したギャラリーを今すぐ直接的に救済することが重要と考えた」とし、「20％の減額が、公正かつ妥当な着地点だと判断した」と続けた。さらに、規模や知名度の大小を問わず、「参加した全てのギャラリーが成功を収められるよう配慮している」との見解を述べている。"}, 「ギャラリー軽視」との批判も。アート・バーゼル・パリ、早期閉幕の補償は「出展料20%引き」

10月下旬に開催された アート・バーゼル・パリ が、大規模な抗議デモや破壊行為への懸念から予定を2日繰り上げて閉幕。それによる機会損失がどう補償されるかが注目される中、11月11日に決定事項が発表された。この問題に関するアート・バーゼル側、出展ディーラー側双方の見解や対応を取材した。

10月24日（土）の抗議デモ計画を受け、予定より2日早く閉幕した アート・バーゼル・パリ 。その措置への補償が、全出展者の最終請求額を20％減額することで決定した。10月24日・25日の開催中止について アート・バーゼル の ノア・ホロウィッツ CEOは、US版ARTnewsの取材にこう答えている。

「早期閉幕という事態への例外的な対応として、 パリ のフェアに参加した全ギャラリーのブース料金を20％減額します」

ようやく出された補償方針は「熟慮の末の公正な対応」

ギャラリー は通常、参加費の大部分を前払いするが、今回はフェア終了後30日以内に発行される最終的な請求書にこの割引が反映される。ただしこれはアート・バーゼルの管理下にない第三者への支払い、いわゆる「特別注文」（照明やブースのカスタマイズなどの費用）には適用されない。たとえば、あるギャラリーのブース料金が1万ドル、ブースのカスタマイズや照明設置などの追加サービス料金が1万ドルだった場合、合計の2万ドルから2000ドルが引かれることになる。ちなみに、中止された日の入場チケットは既に払い戻しが完了している。

アート・バーゼル・パリがセキュリティ上の理由から早期閉幕を発表したのは、前週の17日に続き、24日にも大規模デモの計画があったからだ。出展者はそれ以来、会期短縮への補償に関する主催者の発表を待ち続けていた。特に、小規模ギャラリーや新興ギャラリーにとっては切実な問題だ。

今回のフェアは、10月20日（火）に招待制VIPプレビュー「アヴァン・プレミエール」で幕を開け、21日と22日のVIPデーも招待客限定で実施された。予定会期には土日が含まれていたが、それを待たずに閉幕したため、一般公開されたのは23日（金）の1日だけとなった。ホロウィッツは減額発表についてこう説明している。

「決定に至るまで、約2週間半という時間がかかったことは承知しています。ただ、この措置を講じる前に、あらゆる点を総合的に検討し、ギャラリーの皆さんと適切な調整を行いたいと考えました」

アート・バーゼルは、 マイアミ・ビーチ のフェア（12月2日〜6日、VIPデー含む）の準備を進める中、11月11日に減額を知らせる手紙をパリに出展した全ギャラリーへ送付。同フェアのディレクター、カリム・クリッパの署名がある手紙にはこう書かれていた。

「中止の影響は、ギャラリーごとに異なると理解しています。その上で、今回の措置は、皆さんとのパートナーシップへの感謝と、関係をさらに強めたいという私たちの決意を反映した、熟慮の末の公正な対応だと考えています」

フランス・ギャラリー協会の抗議とアート・バーゼル側の見解

今回の措置が発表されたのは、 フランス のギャラリー協会（CPGA：Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art）がクリッパに送った抗議の書簡が話題になった後のことだった。フェアの会期短縮に対する「公正な補償」を強い表現で求めた10月28日付の同協会の書簡については、 ドイツ のカルチャーメディア、モノポルがいち早く報じている。

CPGAは340以上のギャラリーが加盟する団体で、アート・バーゼル・パリに出展した211ギャラリーのうち57軒が会員だ。書簡の中でCPGAは、主催者が出展者の意見を聞かずに早期閉幕を発表したことについて、出展者を「軽視」または「侮る」（原文のフランス語は「mépris」）行為だと批判した。

US版ARTnewsが匿名を条件に話を聞いたCPGAの主要メンバーによると、主催者と出展者の間で十分な意思疎通がないまま早期閉幕が決まったことに対し、「大きな怒りと当惑」が広がっていたという。この人物はさらにこう続けた。

「難しい決断だったことは分かりますが、誰一人として意見を聞かれなかったのは理解できません。わずか数分の相談すらなかったのです」

10月29日付けで同協会が会員に宛てたメールでも、「こうした決定は、出展ギャラリーの代表者と協議したうえで下すべきだ。しかし、事前の協議は一切なかった」とされている。

24日（土）は抗議デモが予定され、フェア会場である グラン・パレ 前での集会も呼びかけられていたため、この日の中止はやむを得ないとして広く受け入れられた。ところが、出展者の多くは、25日（日）にフェアが再開されなかったことに驚いたという。デモの予定はなく、グラン・パレの別会場でのセザンヌ展は再開されていたからだ。CPGAのフィリップ・シャルパンティエ会長は、フランス版アート・ニュースペーパー紙に対し、次のように語っている。

「土曜日の中止は全面的に支持します。前週末のデモで警備上の不手際があり、その後に深刻な騒乱が起きたことを思えば、絶対に必要な予防措置でした。ただ、日曜日には再開してほしいと伝える機会がなかったことが残念です」

一方のホロウィッツはCPGAの抗議に関し、「極めて流動的な状況の中で対応を迫られていました。フェア期間中も、その後の数週間も、多くのギャラリーと話し合いを重ね、私たちはそこから多くを学びました。どの事業者もそうであるように、さまざまなプロセスを改善し、今後はより良い対応ができるよう努めます」とUS版ARTnewsに述べ、日曜日に再開しなかった理由をこう付け加えた。

「デモの影響がどこまで広がり、どれほど続くのか、グラン・パレへのアクセスがどの程度制限されるのかなど不確実な点が多く、日曜日に安全に再開できるか確信が持てませんでした。また、土曜日に誰もいないグラン・パレに作品を展示したままにすることには、複数の出展者から深い懸念が寄せられていました。これらを踏まえ、早期に閉幕して金曜日の夜から搬出作業を始めることが最も責任ある対応であり、作品の保護はもちろん、ギャラリストや担当チーム、全スタッフ、そして来場者の安全を守るうえで最善の方策だとの結論に達したのです」

ホロウィッツはまた、「全体状況および当事者間の関係」について幅広く話し合うため、12月14日にアート・バーゼル・パリとCPGAの代表者が会合を持つ予定だと述べた。両者は定期的に会合を開いているが、今回は会期短縮による損害の補償についてアート・バーゼル経営陣との協議を求めたCPGAの要請を受けてのものだという。

会合には、フランス文化省とフェア会場であるグラン・パレの運営母体RMN-GP（フランス国立美術館連合−グラン・パレ）の代表者も出席する。両者はUS版ARTnewsの問い合わせに対し、会期短縮の補償としてのブース料減額には関与していないと回答。ホロウィッツも、アート・バーゼルがRMN-GPおよびフランス当局と結んだ契約や保険の内容についてはコメントできないとしている。

フランス文化省の広報担当者は声明で、「私たちの役割は建設的な対話の場をつくることです。それを通じて、ギャラリー、主催者、会場がそれぞれ受けた影響を把握し、今回の出来事から教訓を得ることが目的です」と強調している。

フランス国外の中小ギャラリーは概ね早期閉幕への理解を示す

補償を正式に求めたのはCPGAだけではない。US版ARTnewsは、フランス国外に拠点を置く数十軒の中堅・小規模ギャラリーに、主催者側の対応について尋ねた。その結果、主催者は何らかの補償をすべきかとの質問には、全員が「はい」と答えている。一方、望ましい補償については、小規模ギャラリーへの補償を優先してほしいという意見から、当初の日程の3分の1が短縮されたのだからブース料金の3分の1を返金してほしいという要望まで、内容は多岐にわたった。中には、来年の出展料やブース料金に充当できるバウチャーを求める声もあった。

これに対してホロウィッツは、将来のフェアで使える特典よりも「10月のフェアに出展したギャラリーを今すぐ直接的に救済することが重要と考えた」とし、「20％の減額が、公正かつ妥当な着地点だと判断した」と続けた。さらに、規模や知名度の大小を問わず、「参加した全てのギャラリーが成功を収められるよう配慮している」との見解を述べている。

また、早期閉幕をどう思うかという質問について、ギャラリー関係者の多くは、アート・バーゼルは当時得られた情報を基に最善の決断をしたと考えると答えている。同時にCPGAの要求にも賛同し、出展者のためにロビー活動をしてくれた同協会への感謝を表明。ただし、CPGAの書簡にある、出展者に対する「軽視」といった強い表現は避けていた。

「私たちの利益は十分に守られていると、全員が感じています。個人的には、ギャラリー『モール・シャルパンティエ』代表で、CPGA会長を務めるフィリップ・シャルパンティエが、フランスのギャラリーのみならず私たち全員の考えを代弁してくれていると思います。この問題には適任です」

そう話すのは、ロサンゼルスとニューヨークでギャラリーを運営するフランソワ・ゲバリーだ。彼は、「（CPGAがアート・バーゼルに送った）あの手紙を読み、これ以上強く促す必要はないと感じました」と付け加えている。CPGAは過去にも、フランス政府へのロビー活動で成果を上げてきた。代表的な例が、美術品の売買にかかる税率を5.5％に引き下げさせたことだ。

中堅として存在感のあるゲバリーのギャラリーは、偶然に頼らず事前の計画に沿って重要作品を売ったため、今回のフェアでまずまずの成果を上げている。

「かなり極端で前例のない状況でしたが、ある意味フェアはうまくいったと思います。前半はおおむね計画通りに運び、満足しています。その後あの決定が出されましたが、難しい判断だったはずです」

ただしゲバリーは、「（グラン・パレの）上階にブースを出していた若手ディーラーたちは、そうは受け止めていません。彼らにとって今回の損失は、おそらく私たちよりも吸収しにくいのでしょう」と語った。

週末の開催中止で大きな影響を受けた小規模・新興ギャラリー

フェア主催者の報告によると、10月21日（水）までに306点の作品が総額1億4800万ドル（約236億円）で売れたという。ただしその大半は、フェア前半で出品作を売り切る傾向にある大手ギャラリーの売上だ。対照的に、終盤の数日に商談をまとめることの多い小規模ギャラリーや新興ギャラリーは、日程短縮の打撃が非常に大きかった。中心から外れたエリアや上階には、フェア後半にかけて人が集まる。予算の多くない地元コレクターは、仕事が休みの週末にこうしたギャラリーのブースを訪れるからだ。

その中で、アート・バーゼルに一部返金を正式に求めたと明かしたのは、シカゴとリスボンに拠点を構えるギャラリー「ドキュメント」を運営するアーロン・ジェントだ。2階の回廊にブースを出していた彼は、メール取材に次のように答えている。

「日程の3分の1が短縮され、私たちは大きな影響を受けました。というのも、私たちが主力とするのは、週末に訪れる人たちが買いやすい価格帯である1万ドル（約159万円）以下の作品だからです。ブースを訪れる大半の人々は、私たちが扱っているアーティストのことを知りません。私たちの主な目的は、来場者に彼らの活動を紹介し、将来の展覧会や販売の機会につなげることにあります」

さらに彼は、今考えると主催者は初日の早い時点で閉幕の前倒しを発表し、「可能な限り多くの人々に来場してもらうため」、残りの日程の開場時間を延長すべきだったと付け加えた。

しかし、中には補償の連絡を待つだけで、能動的に働きかけることはできなかったと話すディーラーもいる。 アムステルダム で自身の名を冠したギャラリーを運営するエレン・デ・ブライエンは、 オランダ の小規模ギャラリーのオーナーである自分は、アート・バーゼル・パリに補償を「要求する立場にはない」と述べている。ジョージアのトビリシとドイツのケルンに拠点を置くLCクワイサーの共同経営者も、「アート・バーゼル側から、補償や出展料減額といった解決案が示されるのを待つだけです。特別なこだわりはなく、何らかの補償があれば良いと考えています」と語り、こう続けた。

「ホテル代やパリに出張したスタッフの旅費だけでも、ギャラリーは損失を被っています。ただ、結果的に大きな混乱が起きなかったとしても、懸念が高まる中で週末にパリを訪れるのを見送った人も多かったので、予防措置を講じたのは妥当だったと思います」

今後、アート界の大規模イベントがこうした騒ぎに巻き込まれるのは当たり前のことになるかもしれないと、ディーラーたちは指摘する。ゲバリーはこう言った。

「今、世界は激動の時代にあります。大規模イベントでの混乱は、今後さらに増えるかもしれません。私たちはそれに順応していく必要があるでしょう」（翻訳：野澤朋代）

But Jesse Eisenberg gives a stylish split-personality turn in Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of the Dostoevsky novella. He plays Simon, a nerdily shy and self-effacing computer programmer in a grim futureworld, ignored by his employers and by co-worker Hannah (Mia Wasikowska), with whom he is hopelessly in love. But then his carbon copy, James, arrives, also of course played by Eisenberg. James is a confident alpha-achiever who impresses his bosses and entrances Hannah – to Simon’s gibbering despair.", "links": [{"text": "Jesse Eisenberg", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/jesse-eisenberg"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "9. His dad is Jeff Daniels, a failed novelist and creative writing professor who enviously fell out with his wife, Walt’s mother (Laura Linney), when her own writing career took off. article_text:
10. The Double (2013)

A doppelganger role can be a trap for an actor: either the two roles are not sufficiently distinct, or they are too hammily different, and either way the result can look like a film school graduation project. But Jesse Eisenberg gives a stylish split-personality turn in Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of the Dostoevsky novella. He plays Simon, a nerdily shy and self-effacing computer programmer in a grim futureworld, ignored by his employers and by co-worker Hannah (Mia Wasikowska), with whom he is hopelessly in love. But then his carbon copy, James, arrives, also of course played by Eisenberg. James is a confident alpha-achiever who impresses his bosses and entrances Hannah – to Simon’s gibbering despair.

9. The Squid and the Whale (2005)

Noah Baumbach ’s brutally black-comic movie, based on his own parents’ unhappy relationship, features Eisenberg as the 16-year-old Walt, an unbearably precocious and self-important young man who has inherited all of his father’s pompous mannerisms. His dad is Jeff Daniels, a failed novelist and creative writing professor who enviously fell out with his wife, Walt’s mother (Laura Linney), when her own writing career took off. As Walt leaves the world of childhood behind, this becomes a rare unsympathetic performance for Eisenberg in many ways, and the nerdy mannerisms for which he became famous look spiky, high-handed and charmless – yet the poignant vulnerability is clear enough.

8. Roger Dodger (2002)

This was the teenage Eisenberg’s feature film acting debut, in which his persona of nerdiness, inexperience and bewilderment first arrived in the cinema, along with that patina of self-awareness with which all these things seemed nonetheless to be coated. He is the high school kid Nick, appalled by his own virginity and in dire need of advice on how to make it with girls. He approaches his Lothario uncle Roger – a glorious performance from Campbell Scott – who has just been dumped by his own girlfriend, and, in a frenzy of misogynist rage, Roger takes Nick on a tour of Manhattan’s pickup joints. Eisenberg’s innocence has a charm and openness that Nick’s womaniser lacks. In some ways, he is the opposite of his character in The Squid and the Whale.

7. Adventureland (2009)

Another of the “virgin” performances with which the younger Eisenberg made his name in the indie-adjacent cinema of the 00s, and he cleverly portrays the way in which the lack of sexual experience becomes the very centre of his character’s existence. It’s a coming-of-age story about a guy called James who has gone through a prestigious undergraduate career at college; the world, supposedly, is now his oyster. But he is still a virgin. And to earn cash for grad school he has to take a job in a scuzzy amusement park, ironically or perhaps not ironically called Adventureland, which is to provide education of a different sort and where he falls for his fellow employee, played by Kristen Stewart .

6. Sasquatch Sunset (2024)

It is a film and a role that would challenge any actor: Eisenberg, in full makeup and hairy costume, plays a grunting, nonverbal sasquatch loping through the empty northern California wilderness. He is one of four apelike bigfoot figures who are perhaps the only creatures left alive after some human-made apocalypse, or perhaps we have simply been allowed to share these creatures’ habitual seclusion, their secret existence away from humans. Eisenberg is, perhaps inevitably, the beta-male sasquatch who is less demonstrative than the alpha male grunter. It is a cult performance in a cult film.

5. Café Society (2016)

It was probably Eisenberg’s destiny to work with Woody Allen at some stage – he is in Café Society and, less prominently, in To Rome With Love, from 2012. Café Society is one of Allen’s innumerable light jeux d’ésprit comedies and perhaps not too memorable, but it has a very interesting performance from Eisenberg. He plays a nervy, gauche romantic who is, of course, ventriloquising Allen in the traditional way, but we also see him grow up from boy to man. Set in the US in the 30s, he’s the kid who gets a nepo job in LA as an assistant to his movie-agent uncle and then another in a New York club run by his brother, where he becomes a white-tuxedoed Bogartian figure, nursing a broken heart.

4. Zombieland (2009)

This came out the same year as Adventureland, creating the odd illusion that it was part of some kind of franchise – but no, the two films have nothing to do with each other, although Eisenberg’s appearance in both is not dissimilar; he is, as ever, the shy nerd who is also a potential hottie. (This film was followed up 10 years later by an underpar sequel entitled Zombieland: Double Tap, in which Eisenberg reprised his role.) He plays Columbus, a gauche, brainy guy in a post-apocalyptic landscape infested by zombies. Columbus teams up with Woody Harrelson’s redneck, who is overbearing and moreover keeps ruining his chances of making it with a young woman, played by Emma Stone, who goes on the road with them. His rage with Harrelson results in one of the most entertaining outbursts of Eisenberg’s movie career, as he screams: “You are like a giant, cock-blocking robot developed in some kind of secret government lab!”

3. The Art of Self-Defense (2019)

Film-maker and Brazilian ju-jitsu specialist Riley Stearns created a dark comedy that allowed Eisenberg to explore an interesting possibility to his habitual persona: what if that nerdy, maladroit shyness led not to romcom sexual success, but violence and a general outbreak of toxic masculinity? Eisenberg is Casey, a lonely office worker who is attacked by a gang of bikers and, traumatised, enrols in a karate class. It is led by a charismatic sensei (Alessandro Nivola) whose demands on him become increasingly disturbing.

2. A Real Pain (2024)

This understated, complex, contemporary film is Eisenberg’s directorial masterpiece. He also gives an outstanding performance, all the more interesting in that it is effectively a supporting turn, ceding the spotlight most of the time to Kieran Culkin. (The Polish-set film is also a very personal movie for Eisenberg, who has now taken up Polish citizenship.) Eisenberg plays David, Culkin is his cousin, Benji; the two are on a kind of buddy-movie road trip visit to Poland to visit the childhood home of their late grandmother, who was a Holocaust survivor. Eisenberg plays – inevitably – a strait-laced, uptight figure while Culkin is the more anarchic free spirit, but without the former’s sensibility and maturity, the latter’s performance wouldn’t make sense.

1. The Social Network (2010)

Casting Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg, the young computer genius at Harvard who in 2004 invented Facebook in a frenzy of sexual and social rejection, was a stroke of genius. It allowed Eisenberg to weaponise and make sense of the nerdy onscreen persona that had come so readily to him; it also showed that he was a natural performer of screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s mile-a-minute dialogue. In Eisenberg’s other films, the underdog-nerd aspect was there as a kind of adorable (or perhaps disquieting) flaw, to be surmounted in the course of the narrative. Here it is the whole point. The nerdiness is the superpower; not getting it on with girls is the equivalent of lifting a car above his head. This was the sensational role which was to get Eisenberg the part of ubervillain Lex Luthor in DC films such as Batman V Superman: Dawn of Justice and Zack Snyder’s Justice League and the smart-alec illusionist J Daniel Atlas in the magician-heist caper Now You See Me. But none of those had anything like the quicksilver brilliance of his Zuckerberg, who is entitled and insufferable, driven and obsessive, always convinced of his intellectual superiority, never conceding any point to anyone in any argument, treating everyone to a nonstop fusillade of putdowns and zingers. Eisenberg convinced a whole generation that this was what Mark Zuckerberg was really like. It is a classic performance.

article_text:
Honorable Mention Art + Science Competition: Seth Cook

© Seth Cook, Chromoscape no. 21 (Lake Martin, Midday)

For the Art + Science Competition entitled States of Change , we asked to see photography that examines art and science through transition, transformation, and instability. Change may be gradual or abrupt, visible or difficult to perceive, ranging from emotional shifts to environmental conditions. We invited artists to consider how photography can reveal states of change—where boundaries are not fixed and conditions are continually shifting.

Heavy metals and other chemicals from industrial runoff permeate many of our most splendid and important natural resources. Seth Cook’ s Closer to the Sun merges conservation-centric documentation of the Atchafalaya Basin in Louisiana, with a strong material metaphor. His photographs are made using the chromoskedasic sabattier process, that results in black and white photography with an iridescent gold and silver surface that brings heavy metals and oil slicks to mind. Conceptually, Cook’s chemistry and documentation of a polluted landscape intermingle perfectly.

© Seth Cook,Texaco property sign located in the Atchafalaya Basin

© Seth Cook, The beginning of my journey was thanks to my friend and fellow photographer Kristi Cornell, who helped me make contact with Skip of McGee’s Swamp Tours (Kristi is in the foreground, and Skip is in the background)

“ Closer to the Sun ” is an ongoing photographic study of industrial pollution and the altered landscapes that carry decades of hidden contamination. Drawing on the myth of Icarus, a story of unchecked ambition and its consequences, the work examines regions where industrial progress and environmental vulnerability have become inseparable. Through fieldwork and research, this multi-year project documents industrial legacy across the Mississippi watershed.

The final photographic prints are rendered with the Chromoskedasic Sabattier process, a darkroom technique that manipulates silver particles to produce unpredictable tonal reversals, metallic sheens, and vibrant colors. The process is itself unstable and only partially controllable, a metaphor for humanities impact on the environment. In these prints, contaminated, re-engineered, and quietly poisoned landscapes become both evidence and reflection, revealing how industry reshapes not only the land but the very image of America, highlighting the importance of industrial regulation and the continuation of environmental preservation.

The project began in 2022 with an exploration of the Atchafalaya Basin in Louisiana, America’s largest wetland and the site of active and inactive petrochemical infrastructure. With help from the Atchafalaya Basinkeepers, and later McGee’s Swamp Tours, I was guided through the waterways of the Atchafalaya Basin and documented terminals, control stations, barges, and even stretches of abandoned highway.

In 2026, the project expanded by concentrating on the industrial pollution around Buffalo, NY. Through an artist residency supported by CEPA Gallery, I was able to document the surrounding areas and consider the polluted history behind sites such as Love Canal, Tifft Nature Preserve, and Silo City. That experience influenced the project’s next phase: the entire Mississippi River watershed, centered on Superfund/NPL sites along three corridors, the Arkansas, Missouri, and Ohio Rivers. Each location represents a distinct typology of industrial and agricultural pollution, supplemented by a broader view of the full Mississippi drainage basin.

© Seth Cook, Chromoscape no. 24 (Basin Powerlines) before and after

© Seth Cook, Chromoscape no. 3 (For Lease) before and after

Seth Cook is an artist from the Bayou Teche region in south-central Louisiana. Drawing inspiration from the swamps and marshes of his home, his versatile studio practice often merges photography with other creative media, imbuing a deeper sense of meaning through his choice of materials and techniques. Reviews of his work are featured in publications such as Lenscratch, SHOTS Magazine, and Analog Explorations. His work can be found in the permanent collection of the Museum of Contemporary Art of Georgia and Manifest Gallery and Creative Research Center. He is a recipient of GCSU’s 2026 Academic Affairs Creative Research Grant, the 2024-2025 Digital Humanities Collaborative Grant, and a 2025/2026 Critical Mass Top 200 Finalist. He serves as Assistant Professor of Photography at Georgia College and State University.

About the Jurors:

Linda Alterwitz is an independent interdisciplinary artist with a focus on photography. For over two decades, her work has combined art and science exploring the unseen systems that shape our world and the relationships between humanity, technology, and the natural environment to encourage dialogue around choice, trust, and collective experience. Using a high-resolution thermal camera and other digital and analogue techniques, she visualizes phenomena beyond ordinary perception.

She has exhibited widely in traditional exhibition and site-specific installations at institutions including FORMAT25, Derby, UK; Museum of Art & History, Lancaster, CA – part of PST ART: Art & Science Collide Getty Initiative; New Mexico Museum of Art, Santa Fe, NM, among others.

Alterwitz’s work is held in permanent collections including the Institute for Art + Environment, Reno, NV; Center for Creative Photography, Tucson, AZ; Getty Research Institute, Los Angeles, CA; Hilliard Museum of Art, Lafayette, LA; Nelson Atkins Special Collections Library, Kansas City, MO; Santa Barbara Museum of Art Fearing Library, Santa Barbara, CA; Rochester Institute of Technology, Wallace Library, Rochester, NY, among others.

Recent awards include Nevada Arts Council Fellowship for Visual Arts 2025 and 2014, Individual Artist Grant from Healthy Communities Coalition 2023, NV, Individual Artist Grant 2020, Montana Arts Council, among others.

Instagram: @lindaalterwitz

Ben Hickey is the Executive Director for the Center for Exploratory and Perceptual Arts in Buffalo, New York. Previously he was curator of exhibitions and Emily Cyr Bridges Endowed Professor of Art at the Hilliard Art Museum on the campus of the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. With over one hundred exhibition credits, artists he has exhibited include Brian Kelly of the Marais Press, Letitia Huckaby, L. Kasimu Harris, Robert C. Tannen, Richard Landry, Pat Phillips, Sonya Clark, Hasan Elahi, Dawoud Bey, and James Surls.

Hickey’s most recent writing can be found in Beili Liu: Mend, a monograph published by the Art League Houston in celebration of Liu’s 2024 Texas Artist of the Year Award. Other essayists include Bridget Bray, Annette DiMeo Carlozzi, Eddie Chambers, Katie Pfohl, and Kay Whitney.

In 2023 Hickey received a Samuel H. Kress Foundation Travel Grant to co-present research related to Marais Press on-campus collaborations at the 51st Annual Art Libraries Society of North America in Mexico City. Earlier in his career, he presented Reshaping Our Programming: The Artist in Residence Program at the New York Historical Society in conjunction with an Association of Art Museum Curators annual conference. He has also served as a panelist or consultant for Villa Albertine, the Joan Mitchell Center, Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities, PhotoNOLA, and the San Antonio Art League.

Earlier in his career, Hickey held positions at the Masur Museum of Art, California Museum of Photography, Buffalo AKG Art Museum, and the Arts Council of Buffalo & Erie County. He is an active member of the Association of Art Museum Curators, having served as a trustee from 2015 to 2020. He earned his master’s in art history from the University of California Riverside and his bachelor’s in history from Canisius University.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: It’s been called “beautifully crafted and meticulously composed,” praised by Werner Herzog, awarded at Sundance and honored with five Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations.

On Wednesday, MUBI released the trailer for Nuisance Bear and announced the theatrical release plan for the documentary directed and filmed by Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden : It will open in Los Angeles on November 6 and in New York, Canada and the UK on December 4. Watch the exclusive trailer above.

“For thousands of years, polar bears have migrated along the shores of Hudson Bay in northern Canada,” notes a synopsis. “Today, that ancient rhythm collides with a human world of tourism, surveillance, and control. Nuisance Bear immerses viewers in the experience of a polar bear forced to navigate tourists, wildlife officers, and hunters as climate change delays the freeze and pushes bears closer to human settlements. When a sacred predator is branded a ‘nuisance,’ it becomes unclear who truly belongs in this shared landscape.”

Related Stories

'A Long Winter': Watch First Trailer For Andrew Haigh Drama Starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe & Kit Connor

New York Times Op-Docs Acquires 'The Revolution Against Death,' Oscar Nominee Joshua Oppenheimer's Film On Quest For Immortality

The filmmakers shot Nuisance Bear in Churchill, Manitoba, which calls itself the “Polar Bear Capital of the World.” “[W]ith striking intimacy and scale, the film observes bears that are constantly monitored, photographed, and redirected,” the synopsis continues. “In tracing this uneasy coexistence, Nuisance Bear becomes a meditation on how humans manage, commodify, and redefine wildlife—overturning the conventions of the nature documentary and reframing animals not as spectacle, but as active agents in a rapidly changing world.”

Watch on Deadline

The film is produced by Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden, Will N. Miller, Teddy Leifer, and Michael Code.

“Ultimately, our aim is to collapse the distance between audience and subject,” Weisman and Vanden said in a statement. “By immersing viewers in the bear’s perspective while exposing the human forces shaping every step of its path, we challenge them to see this landscape, both natural and political, as a shared and increasingly contested space. Nuisance Bear invites us to reconsider who truly belongs here and what coexistence demands of all of us.”

Among the many awards for the film are the Grand Jury Prize for U.S. Documentary at the Sundance Film Festival, the 2026 Werner Herzog Film Award, the top prize from the Silk Road International Film Festival in China, and the James Balog Creative Vision Award at Mountainfilm in Telluride, CO. On Tuesday, it was nominated for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Science/Nature Documentary, Best Cinematography and two other awards for the upcoming Critics Choice Documentary Awards.

“From the time we saw the film, we were mesmerized by not only the incredible story of the nuisance bear, but what it says about humanity,” commented Arianna Bocco, Global SVP of Distribution and Acquisitions, MUBI. “The film is beautiful and profound – and we are thrilled to be working with Jack and Gabriela on their stunning feature debut.”

Nuisance Bear is edited by Andres Landau; Cristóbal Tapia De Veer composed the music. Mike Tunalaaq Gibbons narrates the film. Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden serve as directors of photography, with additional cinematography by Sam Holling, Michael Code, Ian Kerr, and Jack Gawthrop. Executive producers include Nicole Stott, Emily Osborne, Harry Go, Nicole Quintero Ochoa, Eric Anoee, Joe Karetak, Alex Pritz, Moudhy Al-Rashid, Sam Frohman, Christine D’Souza, Julia Nelson, Adriana Banta, Emily Goldner, ZZ, and Mike Anders.

Watch the Nuisance Bear trailer above.

title_original: 7 anniversari: il film sull’amore a scadenza della Generazione Z
editorial_title_zh: 7 anniversari: il film sull’amore a scadenza della Generazione Z
editorial_excerpt_zh: 当想象未来变成了一种恐惧，连爱情也在寻找一个期限。在罗马电影节上，萨布丽娜·亚努奇讲述了一个悬置于渴望结合与急于自我保护之间的代际群体。文章《7 anniversari: il film sull’amore a scadenza…》
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "7年的时间，一个承诺和一个注定要说再见的既定日期。在萨布丽娜·亚努奇（Sabrina Iannucci）的导演处女作《7 anniversari》中——该片入围了2026年罗马电影节的“自由风格”（Freestyle）单元——爱情并非关于永恒的承诺，而是一段有期限的经历。这种情感契约在浪漫喜剧的轻盈外表下，捕捉到了Z世代最深层的隐忧之一：无法再想象没有恐惧的未来。", "links": [{"text": "Festa del Cinema di Roma 2026", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/film-e-serie-tv/il-rumore-delle-cose-nuove-lultimo-film-di-genovese-si-muove-nelle-crepe-della-felicita/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.102.1_1-1024x613.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由贝内代塔·波尔卡罗利（Benedetta Porcaroli）饰演的艾玛（Emma）是一名成功的配音演员，而洛伦佐·祖尔佐洛（Lorenzo Zurzolo）饰演的泰奥（Teo）则是一个热爱设计的创意人才，靠送外卖维持生计。他们的相遇几乎纯属偶然，是在一次汉堡配送过程中。双方瞬间被彼此吸引，但在坠入爱河的表象背后，隐藏着不同的脆弱。艾玛带着家庭创伤，这让她难以全身心投入感情；而泰奥似乎更自由地生活在世间，反抗着各种社会习俗与期待。正是他提出了一个既荒谬又具有启发性的解决方案。他们的关系将持续7年，时间一到，两人便可自由分手。对艾玛来说，提前设定好终点意味着中和痛苦的不可预测性。如果离别早已注定，它就再也不会出其不意。因此，这种期限成了一种保护，一个让人安心的框架，在其中甚至可以允许自己奢侈地去爱。这种电影选择折射出了当代青年的生存状况。成长于经历经济危机、就业不稳定以及社会流动性承诺愈发难以兑现的环境中，Z世代所面对的地平线不仅关乎工作上的不安定，更渗透到了身份认同与人际关系之中。学历并不能保证获得与所学路径相符的职业，而工作则面临着变成一种生存工具而非实现个人价值可能性的风险。工作不一定能定义一个人是谁，因为当务之急往往是找到能让自己维持生计的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.18.1_1-1024x610.jpg", "alt": "7 anniversari", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这种背景下，连亲密关系也受到了一种预防性控制。规划共同的生活意味着接受不可预测性、日常的重复、无聊以及对方不可避免的改变。那么，不如设定一个期限，限制投入，减少失去控制的风险。然而，原本为了遏制恐惧而生的事物，最终却在考验它本应保障的自由。随着岁月流逝，泰奥和艾玛的感情超越了契约的边界。随着约定日期的临近，他暗自希望她能改变主意，时间也变成了一种挥之不去的存在。第七个周年纪念日不再仅仅是一个需要履行的承诺，而是对爱情本身意义的一种质问。家庭维度同样塑造了这一情感风景。母亲的形象唤起了一个成年人世界的缩影：有时他们无法自行消化挫折，转而将其转嫁给子女，留下了继续左右未来关系的恐惧遗产。生于1989年的亚努奇保留了纪录片创作经验的痕迹，以一种细腻的敏感度，构建了一部苦乐参半的喜剧，能够将情感视为个体与社会的共同现象。波尔卡罗利和祖尔佐洛自然地展现了一对渴望相爱却又不敢完全交付于不确定性的情侣的种种矛盾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.52.1-1024x611.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《7 anniversari》并没有提供战胜恐惧的公式，而是指出了其中的悖论。在试图避开痛苦的过程中，艾玛和泰奥冒着剥夺当下最真实可能性的风险。对于一个习惯于将所有确定性都视为暂时的时代而言，或许真正的挑战不在于许下永远的诺言，而在于接受没有任何一种关系能够在不承担改变风险的情况下存在。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sette anni, una promessa e una data prestabilita per dirsi addio. In 7 anniversari , opera prima di Sabrina Iannucci , presentata alla Festa del Cinema di Roma 2026 nella sezione Freestyle , l’amore non è una promessa di eternità, ma un’esperienza a termine. Un patto sentimentale che, dietro la leggerezza della commedia romantica, intercetta una delle inquietudini più profonde della Generazione Z, quella di non riuscire più a immaginare il futuro senza esserne spaventati.", "links": [{"text": "Festa del Cinema di Roma 2026", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/film-e-serie-tv/il-rumore-delle-cose-nuove-lultimo-film-di-genovese-si-muove-nelle-crepe-della-felicita/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.102.1_1-1024x613.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emma, interpretata da Benedetta Porcaroli , lavora con successo come doppiatrice, mentre Teo, a cui presta il volto Lorenzo Zurzolo , è un creativo appassionato di design che si mantiene facendo il rider. Il loro incontro avviene quasi per caso, durante una consegna di hamburger. L’attrazione è immediata, ma dietro l’innamoramento si nascondono fragilità differenti. Emma porta con sé ferite familiari che rendono difficile abbandonarsi ai sentimenti, mentre Teo sembra abitare il mondo con maggiore libertà, opponendosi alle convenzioni e alle aspettative sociali. È lui a proporre una soluzione tanto paradossale quanto rivelatrice. La loro relazione durerà sette anni, trascorsi i quali entrambi saranno liberi di lasciarsi. Stabilire in anticipo la fine significa, per Emma, neutralizzare l’imprevedibilità del dolore. Se l’abbandono è già previsto, non può più cogliere di sorpresa. Il limite diventa così una protezione, una cornice rassicurante entro cui concedersi persino il lusso di amare. La scelta cinematografica racconta molto della condizione giovanile contemporanea. Cresciuta attraversando crisi economiche, instabilità occupazionale e promesse di mobilità sociale sempre più difficili da mantenere, la Generazione Z si confronta con un orizzonte in cui la precarietà non riguarda soltanto il lavoro, ma investe l’identità e le relazioni. Il titolo di studio non garantisce una professione coerente con il percorso compiuto, mentre l’occupazione rischia di trasformarsi in uno strumento di sopravvivenza più che in una possibilità di realizzazione personale. Il lavoro non definisce necessariamente chi si è, perché spesso la priorità consiste nel trovare ciò che permette di restare a galla."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.18.1_1-1024x610.jpg", "alt": "7 anniversari", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In questo scenario, anche l’intimità viene sottoposta a una forma di controllo preventivo. Progettare una vita insieme significa accettare l’imprevisto, la ripetizione quotidiana, la noia e le inevitabili trasformazioni dell’altro. Meglio, allora, stabilire una scadenza, delimitare il coinvolgimento, ridurre il rischio di perdere il controllo. Ma ciò che nasce per contenere la paura finisce per mettere alla prova proprio la libertà che dovrebbe garantire. Mentre gli anni passano, i sentimenti di Teo ed Emma crescono oltre i confini del patto. Lui spera segretamente che lei cambi idea, mentre la data concordata si avvicina, trasformando il tempo in una presenza costante. Il settimo anniversario non è più soltanto una promessa da mantenere, ma una domanda sul significato stesso dell’amore. Anche la dimensione familiare contribuisce a definire questo paesaggio emotivo. La figura materna richiama un mondo adulto incapace, talvolta, di elaborare le proprie frustrazioni senza trasferirle sui figli, lasciando in eredità paure che continuano a condizionare le relazioni future. Con una sensibilità che conserva tracce della sua esperienza nel cinema documentario, Iannucci, classe 1989, costruisce una commedia dolceamara capace di osservare i sentimenti come fenomeni individuali e, insieme, sociali. Porcaroli e Zurzolo restituiscono con naturalezza le contraddizioni di una coppia che desidera amare senza consegnarsi completamente all’incertezza."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/7A_1.52.1-1024x611.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "7 anniversari non offre una formula per superare la paura, ma ne individua il paradosso. Nel tentativo di evitare il dolore, Emma e Teo rischiano di sottrarre al presente la sua possibilità più autentica. Per una generazione abituata a considerare ogni certezza provvisoria, forse la sfida non consiste nel promettersi per sempre, ma nell’accettare che nessun legame possa essere vissuto senza esporsi al rischio del cambiamento."}]
article_text:
Sette anni, una promessa e una data prestabilita per dirsi addio. In 7 anniversari , opera prima di Sabrina Iannucci , presentata alla Festa del Cinema di Roma 2026 nella sezione Freestyle , l’amore non è una promessa di eternità, ma un’esperienza a termine. Un patto sentimentale che, dietro la leggerezza della commedia romantica, intercetta una delle inquietudini più profonde della Generazione Z, quella di non riuscire più a immaginare il futuro senza esserne spaventati.

Emma, interpretata da Benedetta Porcaroli , lavora con successo come doppiatrice, mentre Teo, a cui presta il volto Lorenzo Zurzolo , è un creativo appassionato di design che si mantiene facendo il rider. Il loro incontro avviene quasi per caso, durante una consegna di hamburger. L’attrazione è immediata, ma dietro l’innamoramento si nascondono fragilità differenti. Emma porta con sé ferite familiari che rendono difficile abbandonarsi ai sentimenti, mentre Teo sembra abitare il mondo con maggiore libertà, opponendosi alle convenzioni e alle aspettative sociali. È lui a proporre una soluzione tanto paradossale quanto rivelatrice. La loro relazione durerà sette anni, trascorsi i quali entrambi saranno liberi di lasciarsi. Stabilire in anticipo la fine significa, per Emma, neutralizzare l’imprevedibilità del dolore. Se l’abbandono è già previsto, non può più cogliere di sorpresa. Il limite diventa così una protezione, una cornice rassicurante entro cui concedersi persino il lusso di amare. La scelta cinematografica racconta molto della condizione giovanile contemporanea. Cresciuta attraversando crisi economiche, instabilità occupazionale e promesse di mobilità sociale sempre più difficili da mantenere, la Generazione Z si confronta con un orizzonte in cui la precarietà non riguarda soltanto il lavoro, ma investe l’identità e le relazioni. Il titolo di studio non garantisce una professione coerente con il percorso compiuto, mentre l’occupazione rischia di trasformarsi in uno strumento di sopravvivenza più che in una possibilità di realizzazione personale. Il lavoro non definisce necessariamente chi si è, perché spesso la priorità consiste nel trovare ciò che permette di restare a galla.

In questo scenario, anche l’intimità viene sottoposta a una forma di controllo preventivo. Progettare una vita insieme significa accettare l’imprevisto, la ripetizione quotidiana, la noia e le inevitabili trasformazioni dell’altro. Meglio, allora, stabilire una scadenza, delimitare il coinvolgimento, ridurre il rischio di perdere il controllo. Ma ciò che nasce per contenere la paura finisce per mettere alla prova proprio la libertà che dovrebbe garantire. Mentre gli anni passano, i sentimenti di Teo ed Emma crescono oltre i confini del patto. Lui spera segretamente che lei cambi idea, mentre la data concordata si avvicina, trasformando il tempo in una presenza costante. Il settimo anniversario non è più soltanto una promessa da mantenere, ma una domanda sul significato stesso dell’amore. Anche la dimensione familiare contribuisce a definire questo paesaggio emotivo. La figura materna richiama un mondo adulto incapace, talvolta, di elaborare le proprie frustrazioni senza trasferirle sui figli, lasciando in eredità paure che continuano a condizionare le relazioni future. Con una sensibilità che conserva tracce della sua esperienza nel cinema documentario, Iannucci, classe 1989, costruisce una commedia dolceamara capace di osservare i sentimenti come fenomeni individuali e, insieme, sociali. Porcaroli e Zurzolo restituiscono con naturalezza le contraddizioni di una coppia che desidera amare senza consegnarsi completamente all’incertezza.

7 anniversari non offre una formula per superare la paura, ma ne individua il paradosso. Nel tentativo di evitare il dolore, Emma e Teo rischiano di sottrarre al presente la sua possibilità più autentica. Per una generazione abituata a considerare ogni certezza provvisoria, forse la sfida non consiste nel promettersi per sempre, ma nell’accettare che nessun legame possa essere vissuto senza esporsi al rischio del cambiamento.
